aliases: Securities and Exchange Board of India
hl: securities and exchange board of india
short: India's regulator for the stock and bond markets, which writes and enforces the rules for exchanges, brokers, mutual funds and listed companies.
kid: SEBI is like the referee at a playground game. It makes the rules, watches that nobody cheats, and stops players who break the rules.
detail: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is the statutory regulator of India's securities markets. Set up in 1988 and given legal powers by the SEBI Act, 1992, it has three jobs: protect investors, develop the market and regulate it. It registers and supervises stock exchanges, depositories, clearing corporations, brokers, mutual funds, foreign portfolio investors and research analysts; reviews IPO documents; and polices insider trading, price manipulation and takeovers. It can investigate, impose penalties, bar people from the market and order money to be returned, and appeals against its orders go to the Securities Appellate Tribunal. SEBI decisions, such as the move to T+1 settlement and tighter rules on futures and options for retail traders, shape how everyone trades. Common confusion: SEBI does not regulate banks (the RBI does), insurers (IRDAI) or pension funds (PFRDA), and it never guarantees that any investment will make money.
example: Say ABC Ltd plans a ₹600 crore IPO, made up of ₹400 crore of new shares and a ₹200 crore offer for sale by existing investors. Before it can open, ABC must file a draft offer document with SEBI, which checks that risks and finances are fully disclosed. SEBI does not decide whether the price is fair; investors must judge that themselves.

short: India's largest stock exchange by trading volume, where shares, bonds, index futures and options and other securities are bought and sold electronically.
kid: Imagine a giant, busy fair where people swap toys all day, and a helper writes down every swap so nobody gets tricked. NSE is a fair like that, but on computers.
detail: The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE), based in Mumbai, was set up in 1992 and began trading in 1994 as the country's first nationwide, fully automated, screen-based exchange. It moved Indian trading away from crowded trading floors and made it possible to trade from anywhere in the country. NSE runs markets in equities, equity derivatives, currency derivatives, debt and commodities, and its flagship index is the Nifty 50. It handles the large majority of India's equity cash trading and is one of the world's largest derivatives exchanges by number of contracts traded. Its group includes NSE Clearing, which guarantees settlement, and NSE International Exchange in GIFT City. Common confusion: most large companies are listed on both NSE and BSE, so the same share trades on two exchanges at nearly identical prices; and the exchange is only the marketplace, not the seller of the shares.
example: Say you buy 10 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹1,250 each on NSE. You pay 10 x ₹1,250 = ₹12,500 plus brokerage and charges, NSE Clearing guarantees the trade, and under India's T+1 settlement cycle (the rule as of 2025) the shares reach your demat account the next trading day.

short: Asia's oldest stock exchange, set up in 1875 in Mumbai, home of the Sensex and of more listed companies than any other Indian exchange.
kid: BSE is like the oldest shop in town where people come to swap things. It has been open longer than anyone's great-great-grandparents can remember.
detail: BSE Ltd, formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange, grew out of brokers who met under banyan trees in Bombay in the 1850s and was formally organised in 1875, making it Asia's oldest stock exchange. Today it is a fully electronic exchange offering equities, derivatives, mutual fund distribution through BSE StAR MF, an SME platform and an international exchange, India INX, in GIFT City. Its best-known index is the Sensex, which tracks 30 large companies. BSE lists far more companies than NSE, many of them small and thinly traded, though NSE handles much more of the daily trading volume. BSE is itself a listed company whose shares trade on NSE. Common confusion: BSE is the exchange and the Sensex is its index, so when people casually say 'the BSE fell 1%', they mean the Sensex fell.
example: Say ABC Ltd's shares are listed on both BSE and NSE and trade at ₹500.40 on BSE and ₹500.10 on NSE. The 30 paise gap (₹500.40 - ₹500.10 = ₹0.30) stays tiny because arbitrage traders buy on the cheaper exchange and sell on the dearer one until prices line up.

short: NSE's main index, tracking 50 of India's largest, most traded companies; a quick gauge of how the Indian stock market is doing.
kid: Imagine checking how 50 of the biggest shops in town did today by looking at one score. If the score goes up, most of the big shops had a good day.
detail: The Nifty 50 is the National Stock Exchange's flagship index, maintained by NSE Indices. It contains 50 large, liquid companies across major sectors and is weighted by free-float market capitalisation, so a company's influence depends on the value of shares actually available to the public, not just its total size. The index started at a base value of 1,000 on 3 November 1995, and its members are reviewed twice a year. It is the benchmark most Indian large-cap funds are measured against, it is tracked by many index funds and ETFs, and its futures and options are among the most traded contracts in the world. Common confusion: a rise in the Nifty does not mean all 50 stocks rose; a few heavyweight stocks can lift the index while most members fall. Index points are also not rupees.
example: The Nifty 50 began at a base value of 1,000 on 3 November 1995. Say one stock carries a 10% weight in the index and rises 5% in a day while the other 49 are flat: the index rises by 0.10 x 5% = 0.5%.
formula: Index level = Current free-float market cap of constituents / Base market cap x 1,000 (base adjusted for corporate actions and changes in membership)

short: BSE's benchmark index of 30 large, well-established Indian companies, India's oldest widely followed stock index and a shorthand for the market's mood.
kid: Picture 30 big, old shops in town. The Sensex is one number that tells you if those 30 shops, taken together, had a good or a bad day.
detail: The Sensex, short for Sensitive Index, is BSE's flagship index of 30 large, financially sound and actively traded companies drawn from key sectors. First published in 1986 with 1978-79 as its base year and a base value of 100, it is India's oldest widely followed stock index. Since 2003 it has been weighted by free-float market capitalisation, so the value of shares available to the public decides each company's influence. It was branded S&P BSE Sensex during a long tie-up with S&P Dow Jones Indices. Headlines often quote the Sensex and Nifty 50 together; because both are dominated by the same large companies, they usually move in the same direction by similar percentages. Common confusion: compare moves in percentages, not points, because a 500-point fall means far less at a high index level than it did decades ago.
example: Say the Sensex is at 50,000 and falls 500 points: the drop is 500 / 50,000 = 1%. The same 500-point fall when the index stood at 1,000 would have wiped out 500 / 1,000 = 50% of its value.
formula: Index level = Current free-float market cap of the 30 constituents / Base market cap x 100 (base adjusted for corporate actions and changes in membership)

short: An NSE index tracking the largest and most traded Indian bank stocks; its official name is the Nifty Bank index.
kid: Imagine one score for the big places in town that look after everyone's piggy-bank coins. When people feel good about those places, the score goes up.
detail: Bank Nifty, officially the Nifty Bank index, is maintained by NSE Indices and tracks the most liquid, large Indian banks, private and public sector, weighted by free-float market capitalisation. Because banks make up a large slice of the Nifty 50 and react quickly to interest rates, loan growth and bad-loan news, Bank Nifty is closely watched around RBI policy meetings and bank results. It is also one of India's most important derivatives underlyings: its options were for years among the most traded contracts in the world. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, each exchange may offer weekly expiries on only one benchmark index, so from November 2024 NSE kept weekly options on the Nifty 50 and moved Bank Nifty to monthly expiry. In 2025 SEBI also set membership and weight limits for such derivative-linked indices. Common confusion: Bank Nifty excludes non-bank lenders and insurers; those sit in Fin Nifty.
example: Say one bank carries a 20% weight in Bank Nifty and its shares fall 5% after weak results while the other members are flat. The index falls by 0.20 x 5% = 1%, showing how much a single heavyweight can move it.

short: NSE's index of large financial companies, including banks, non-bank lenders, insurers and other financial firms; officially the Nifty Financial Services index.
kid: Bank Nifty looks only at the big places that keep piggy-bank coins. Fin Nifty also looks at helpers who lend coins to people and helpers who fix things when they break, so it is a bigger family.
detail: Fin Nifty, officially the Nifty Financial Services index, is maintained by NSE Indices and tracks large, liquid Indian companies across the financial sector: banks, non-banking financial companies, housing finance companies, insurers, and capital-market firms such as exchanges and asset managers. Like other Nifty indices it is weighted by free-float market capitalisation, with caps that stop any single company from dominating. Derivatives on it were launched in January 2021 and quickly became popular with options traders; under SEBI's limit of one weekly expiry per exchange, in force since November 2024 and as of 2025, its options trade on monthly expiries only. Investors use it to judge the wider financial sector, not just banks. Common confusion: Fin Nifty and Bank Nifty overlap heavily, since big banks are large members of both, so they often move together; the difference shows up when non-bank lenders or insurers move on their own news.
example: Say, in a simplified financial-services index, banks and non-bank lenders make up 80% of the weight and insurers 20%. If lenders fall 2% and insurers rise 2%, the index moves 0.8 x (-2%) + 0.2 x 2% = -1.6% + 0.4% = -1.2%, while a bank-only index would fall the full 2%.

short: An NSE index of the 50 companies ranked just below the Nifty 50 by size, often seen as the next generation of large companies.
kid: Think of a race where the first 50 runners get gold stars. This score watches the next 50 runners, some of whom may win gold stars soon.
detail: The Nifty Next 50, earlier called Nifty Junior, tracks the 50 companies that sit in the Nifty 100 but not in the Nifty 50: roughly the 51st to 100th largest eligible companies on NSE, weighted by free-float market capitalisation. Together, the Nifty 50 and Nifty Next 50 make up the Nifty 100, the large-cap universe. Because companies graduate into the Nifty 50 from this group, and older giants sometimes drop down into it, the index is often described as a pipeline of future leaders. It tends to be more volatile than the Nifty 50 and can be concentrated in a few sectors or in companies with low free float. Index funds and ETFs on it are popular with long-term investors who want large-cap exposure beyond the top 50. Common confusion: it is not a midcap index; its members are mostly large caps under SEBI's fund categories.
example: Say you split ₹1 lakh equally between a Nifty 50 index fund and a Nifty Next 50 index fund. If the first rises 10% and the second 20% over a year, your money grows to ₹55,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹1,15,000, a 15% gain.

short: An NSE index of 500 large, mid-sized and small companies, covering most of the value of India's listed stock market.
kid: The Nifty 50 looks at only the biggest 50 shops in town. The Nifty 500 looks at 500 shops, big, middle and small, so it shows how almost the whole town is doing.
detail: The Nifty 500 is NSE's broad-market index of the top 500 eligible companies ranked by full market capitalisation, weighted by free-float market capitalisation. It is built from three layers: the Nifty 100 (large caps), the Nifty Midcap 150 and the Nifty Smallcap 250, matching the size bands SEBI uses to classify mutual fund schemes. Because it covers the large majority of the free-float value of NSE-listed shares, it is a common benchmark for flexi-cap and other diversified equity funds and gives a fuller picture of the market than the Nifty 50. Large caps still dominate its weight, so its daily moves usually resemble the Nifty 50's, with gaps when mid and small caps diverge. Common confusion: it is not the Nifty Total Market index, which adds 250 microcaps for 750 companies in all.
example: Say large caps make up 70% of the Nifty 500's weight, midcaps 20% and smallcaps 10%. If on one day large caps rise 1%, midcaps 2% and smallcaps 3%, the index rises 0.7% + 0.4% + 0.3% = 1.4%, more than the 1% gain in large caps alone.

short: Indices that track mid-sized and smaller companies beyond the headline Nifty 50 and Sensex, such as the Nifty Midcap 150 and Nifty Smallcap 250.
kid: The race with the biggest kids gets on the news, but lots of middle-sized and little kids are racing too. These scores tell you how the middle and little runners are doing.
detail: Broader market indices measure the part of the stock market beyond the largest companies. NSE's Nifty Midcap 150 covers companies ranked 101st to 250th by full market capitalisation and the Nifty Smallcap 250 those ranked 251st to 500th, mirroring SEBI's size bands for mutual funds, which are refreshed every six months from AMFI's ranking. The older Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 are narrower versions, and BSE runs its own midcap and smallcap indices. When news says 'the broader markets outperformed', it means these indices beat the Nifty 50 or Sensex. Mid and small caps usually rise more in bull runs and fall harder in sell-offs, and they are less liquid, so wide gaps between them and the benchmark can signal speculative excess or panic. Common confusion: a record high in the Nifty 50 says little about how a typical smaller stock is doing.
example: Say in one week the Nifty 50 rises 1%, the Nifty Midcap 150 rises 3% and the Nifty Smallcap 250 falls 2%. Midcaps beat the benchmark by 3 - 1 = 2 percentage points, while smallcaps lagged it by 1 - (-2) = 3 percentage points, so the broader market was mixed.

short: Indices that track the shares of one industry, such as IT, pharma, banks, autos or metals, to show how that sector is performing.
kid: Imagine sorting your toys into boxes: cars in one, dolls in another, blocks in a third. A sector score tells you how one box of toys is doing.
detail: A sectoral index tracks companies from a single industry. NSE's family includes Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma, Nifty FMCG, Nifty Auto, Nifty Metal, Nifty Realty, Nifty PSU Bank and Bank Nifty, and BSE runs equivalents such as Bankex. Each is usually weighted by free-float market capitalisation, so a handful of leaders can dominate: an IT index may in effect be a bet on a few large software exporters. Investors use sectoral indices to compare industries, spot sector rotation (money moving from, say, IT into banks), benchmark sector funds and ETFs, and judge whether a stock's move is company-specific or sector-wide. Sectors respond to different drivers: IT to the rupee and US demand, metals to global commodity prices, banks to interest rates and bad loans. Common confusion: a sectoral index covers one industry, while a thematic index, such as consumption or public sector companies, spans many industries.
example: Say on one day the Nifty IT rises 2.5% after the rupee weakens while the Nifty Metal falls 1.5%. The gap between the two sectors is 2.5 - (-1.5) = 4 percentage points, which can signal money rotating between sectors rather than the whole market moving together.

short: NSE's volatility index, which uses Nifty 50 option prices to show how big a move traders expect over the next 30 days.
kid: Before a storm, the sky gets dark and everyone gets a bit worried. India VIX is like a worry meter: it goes up when people expect big bumps ahead.
detail: India VIX is a volatility index calculated by NSE since 2008 using a method adapted from the CBOE VIX in the US. It uses the best bid and ask prices of near-month and next-month Nifty 50 options to estimate the annualised volatility, in percent, that traders expect over the next 30 calendar days. Because options get expensive when traders rush to buy protection, India VIX tends to jump when markets fall sharply or before uncertain events such as elections and budgets, earning it the nickname 'fear gauge'. Options traders watch it because higher volatility means higher option premiums. Common confusion: India VIX shows the expected size of moves, not their direction, and it is forward-looking (implied) rather than a record of past price swings. A low reading signals calm, not safety. It is also separate from the US VIX, which is based on S&P 500 options.
example: Say India VIX reads 16. Traders are pricing an annualised move of about 16% in the Nifty 50, which is roughly 16 / sqrt(12) = 4.6% over the next month, or 16 / sqrt(252) = about 1.0% on a typical day, in either direction.
formula: Expected 30-day move (approx.) = India VIX / sqrt(12); expected one-day move (approx.) = India VIX / sqrt(252)

short: Dollar-priced Nifty 50 futures traded at GIFT City for most of the day and night, watched as an early hint of India's market opening.
kid: Some grown-ups stay up almost all night guessing how tomorrow's big game will go. In the morning, everyone peeks at their guesses to see if it might be a good day.
detail: GIFT Nifty is the name for Nifty 50 index futures traded on NSE International Exchange (NSE IX) in GIFT City, Gujarat. They are priced and settled in US dollars and trade in two long sessions covering most of the day and night, so they react to US and Asian news while Indian exchanges are shut. They replaced SGX Nifty, which traded on the Singapore Exchange: in July 2023 that trading moved to GIFT City under the NSE IX-SGX Connect, bringing offshore trading in Nifty contracts under Indian jurisdiction. Market reports use GIFT Nifty before the Indian market opens to predict a gap-up or gap-down start. Common confusion: GIFT Nifty is a futures price, so it carries a small premium over the spot index and is best compared with the previous Nifty futures price, not the Nifty 50 close; early signals can also fade by the opening bell.
example: Say Nifty 50 futures in India closed at 20,000 and GIFT Nifty trades at 20,140 the next morning. That is 140 points higher, or 140 / 20,000 = 0.7%, so reports would flag a likely gap-up opening, though the signal can fade before the market opens.

short: Gujarat International Finance Tec-City near Gandhinagar, home to India's International Financial Services Centre, a special zone for offshore-style finance in foreign currency.
kid: GIFT City is a special neighbourhood in India where people from all over the world can play using their own kinds of coins. It has its own rule-maker who keeps things fair.
detail: GIFT City (Gujarat International Finance Tec-City) is a planned business district near Gandhinagar, Gujarat, that houses India's first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). Business inside the IFSC is largely done in foreign currency and treated as offshore for exchange-control purposes, letting India compete with hubs such as Singapore and Dubai. It hosts two international exchanges, NSE IX and India INX, a bullion exchange, bank branches, fund managers, insurers, and aircraft and ship lessors. A single regulator, the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), set up in 2020, oversees finance in the zone in place of the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, and tax incentives apply under the rules as of 2025. Common confusion: GIFT City is the place, the IFSC is the special zone within it, and IFSCA is its regulator; this IFSC has nothing to do with the IFSC code used for bank transfers.
example: Under the rules as of 2025, an eligible IFSC unit can claim a 100% deduction on its qualifying business income for any 10 consecutive years out of its first 15. Say ABC Fund Services Ltd in GIFT IFSC earns ₹15 crore of qualifying profit in one of those years: its taxable income from that business under the normal provisions is ₹15 crore - ₹15 crore = ₹0, although a minimum alternate tax may still apply.

short: National Securities Depository Limited, India's first depository, which holds investors' shares and bonds in electronic form and records who owns them.
kid: NSDL is like a giant, safe notebook that writes down which toys belong to which child. Toys never get lost because the notebook always remembers who owns what.
detail: NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) began operating in 1996, after the Depositories Act of that year, as India's first depository, promoted by IDBI, UTI and NSE. A depository holds securities in electronic (dematerialised) form and keeps the official record of who owns them, so transfers happen by book entry instead of paper certificates. Investors do not deal with NSDL directly; they open demat accounts through depository participants such as banks and brokers. As of 2025, NSDL holds the larger share of the value of securities in Indian demat accounts, reflecting its strong base among institutions, while CDSL has more individual accounts. It also publishes widely watched data on foreign portfolio investor flows. Common confusion: NSDL holds securities, not cash, and your shares are recorded in your own name there, so they remain yours even if your broker fails.
example: Say you hold 100 shares of ABC Ltd worth ₹250 each, or 100 x ₹250 = ₹25,000, in a demat account opened through a broker linked to NSDL. If the broker shuts down, those 100 shares still sit in your name in NSDL's records, and you can move them to another depository participant.

short: Central Depository Services (India) Limited, India's second depository, which holds shares electronically and, as of 2025, maintains more demat accounts than NSDL.
kid: CDSL is another big, safe notebook that writes down which toys belong to which child. Lots and lots of children have their toys listed in this notebook.
detail: CDSL (Central Depository Services (India) Limited) is India's second depository, promoted by BSE, which began operating in 1999. Like NSDL, it holds securities in dematerialised form and records ownership, while investors reach it through depository participants, usually their brokers. CDSL grew fastest during the post-2020 boom in retail investing because many app-based brokers chose it, so as of 2025 it maintains more demat accounts than NSDL, although NSDL holds more value. CDSL itself is listed on NSE. It runs investor-facing services such as e-voting and TPIN-based authorisation for selling shares from a demat account. Common confusion: it makes little difference to an investor whether a demat account sits with CDSL or NSDL; both are SEBI-regulated market infrastructure institutions, and holdings can be moved between them. A CDSL account ID is a 16-digit number, while an NSDL ID starts with 'IN'.
example: Say you sell 40 of your 100 shares of ABC Ltd through a broker linked to CDSL. You authorise the debit with your CDSL TPIN and a one-time password, CDSL moves the 40 shares out for delivery, and your holding drops to 100 - 40 = 60 shares.

short: An account that holds your shares, bonds, ETFs and other securities in electronic form, much as a bank account holds your money.
kid: It is like a special toy box with your name on it, kept safe by grown-ups. Instead of the toys themselves, it keeps a list of every toy you own.
detail: A demat (dematerialised) account holds securities in electronic form with a depository, NSDL or CDSL, and is opened through a depository participant such as a broker or bank. Dematerialisation means converting old paper share certificates into electronic entries. Since April 2019, SEBI rules have required shares of listed companies to be in demat form before they can be transferred, so in practice a demat account is essential for investing in Indian shares, ETFs and listed bonds; mutual fund units can be held either way. When you buy, shares are credited after settlement; when you sell, they are debited. Common confusion: the demat account holds securities, the trading account places orders and the bank account holds cash. Most brokers bundle them, but they are separate. Charges include an annual maintenance fee and a DP fee each time shares leave the account.
example: Say you buy 20 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹300 each through your trading account. ₹6,000 is paid from your linked balance, and after settlement the 20 shares appear in your demat account; if the price later rises to ₹330, your demat statement shows a holding worth 20 x ₹330 = ₹6,600.

short: An account with a stockbroker used to place buy and sell orders on stock exchanges; it works alongside a demat account and a bank account.
kid: To get a toy from the big fair, you tell a helper what you want and the helper fetches it for you. This is how you talk to that helper.
detail: A trading account is opened with a SEBI-registered stockbroker and lets you place orders to buy and sell shares, ETFs, futures, options and other exchange-traded products. When you place an order, the broker sends it to the exchange, which matches it with another investor's order; the clearing corporation then settles the trade, moving money through your trading account and shares into or out of your demat account. Most Indian brokers offer a combined trading and demat (2-in-1) account linked to your bank account, opened after KYC checks. Trading accounts also handle margin for intraday and derivatives trades and generate a contract note for each trade. Common confusion: a trading account does not hold your shares; the demat account does. In school accounting, 'trading account' also means the statement that works out a business's gross profit, which is a different thing entirely.
example: Say you add ₹10,000 to your trading account and buy 25 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹380. The order uses 25 x ₹380 = ₹9,500, leaving ₹500 as available balance before brokerage and charges, while the shares themselves land in your demat account.

short: A SEBI-registered agent, such as a bank or broker, through which investors open and operate demat accounts with NSDL or CDSL.
kid: The big toy notebook is kept far away, so you ask a friendly helper nearby to write in it for you. That helper is the one you talk to.
detail: A depository participant (DP) is the go-between for an investor and a depository. Depositories such as NSDL and CDSL do not open accounts for the public; instead, SEBI-registered DPs, which include banks, stockbrokers and financial institutions, open demat accounts, process transfers, pledges and nominations, and send statements. Each DP has a DP ID, which together with your client ID forms your demat account number. DPs earn fees: an account opening or annual maintenance charge, and DP charges each time securities are debited from your account, usually when you sell. DP charges are a flat fee per company (scrip) per day, not per share, so selling a small quantity can be expensive in percentage terms. Common confusion: your broker and your DP are often the same firm, but the roles differ; the broker executes trades, while the DP keeps your holdings recorded at the depository.
example: Say your DP charges ₹15 per company per day on sales, plus GST. Selling 10 shares of ABC Ltd and 500 shares of XYZ Ltd on the same day costs 2 x ₹15 = ₹30 before GST, because the fee depends on the number of companies, not shares. On a ₹1,000 sale of a single company, ₹15 is already 1.5%.

short: The core plumbing of India's securities markets: stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories, which SEBI regulates more strictly than other market players.
kid: For a game to work, you need a field to play on, a scorekeeper and a safe box for the prizes. These are the field, scorekeeper and prize box of the grown-ups' swapping game.
detail: Market infrastructure institutions (MIIs) is SEBI's term for the entities that form the backbone of the securities market: stock exchanges (such as NSE, BSE and MCX), clearing corporations (such as NSE Clearing and Indian Clearing Corporation) and depositories (NSDL and CDSL). Exchanges match buy and sell orders, clearing corporations guarantee and settle trades so that one side's default does not hurt the other, and depositories record ownership. Because a failure at an MII could freeze the whole market, SEBI treats them as systemically important: they face strict ownership caps, must have public interest directors on their boards, must keep regulatory functions separate from business ones, and must meet high standards for technology, cyber security and outage reporting. MIIs also act as first-line regulators of their members. Common confusion: brokers, depository participants and mutual funds are intermediaries, not MIIs.
example: When you buy 50 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹200, three MIIs handle the 50 x ₹200 = ₹10,000 trade: the exchange matches your order, the clearing corporation guarantees and settles the ₹10,000 payment against the 50 shares, and the depository moves the shares into your demat account.

short: An overseas investor, such as a foreign fund, that registers with SEBI to buy Indian shares and bonds for investment rather than control.
kid: Children from faraway towns sometimes buy a small part of our lemonade stand, hoping it does well. They can buy in and sell out quickly, without ever running the stand.
detail: A foreign portfolio investor (FPI) is a non-resident entity, such as a pension fund, mutual fund, sovereign wealth fund or hedge fund, registered with SEBI under the FPI Regulations, 2019, to invest in Indian listed shares, bonds and other securities. The category replaced the older foreign institutional investor (FII) label in 2014, which is why news still says 'FIIs'. Under the rules as of 2025, a single FPI, together with its investor group, must hold less than 10% of a company's equity; crossing that line turns the holding into foreign direct investment (FDI). FPI money is large and mobile, so its buying and selling moves share prices, bond yields and the rupee, and it is tracked daily. Common confusion: FPI is portfolio investment that can leave quickly, while FDI is a lasting stake in running a business, such as building a factory or buying control.
example: Say a foreign fund registered as an FPI owns 9% of ABC Ltd. Under the rules as of 2025 it can add only a little under 1% more; if it buys 2%, taking its stake to 9% + 2% = 11%, it must either sell the excess within the set deadline or have the holding reclassified as FDI.

short: An Indian institution, such as a mutual fund, insurance company, bank or pension fund, that invests in Indian financial markets.
kid: Lots of families in our town put a few coins each into one big jar every month. Helpers use that jar to buy parts of local lemonade stands for everyone.
detail: Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) are India-based institutions that invest large pools of money, mainly mutual funds, insurance companies such as LIC, banks, and pension and provident funds. Exchanges classify them separately from foreign portfolio investors and from individuals when they publish daily flow data. Their influence has grown sharply as millions of households invest through monthly SIPs in mutual funds, giving DIIs a steady stream of cash to put to work whatever the market's mood. In periods of heavy foreign selling, such as 2022 and late 2024, strong DII buying cushioned Indian markets. Common confusion: DII money is largely ordinary savers' money pooled through funds, so individuals take part both directly and through DIIs; and promoters or companies buying their own shares are not counted as DIIs.
example: Say on one day FPIs sell a net ₹3,000 crore of Indian shares and DIIs buy a net ₹3,500 crore. Domestic buying more than absorbs the foreign selling, by ₹3,500 crore - ₹3,000 crore = ₹500 crore, which helps explain why the index may hold steady.

short: Daily figures on Indian shares bought and sold by foreign and domestic institutions, showing whether each group was a net buyer or seller.
kid: At the end of each day, someone counts what visitors from far away bought and sold at the fair, and what local families bought and sold. Then everyone can see which group was keener that day.
detail: FII and DII data are the daily net flows of foreign institutional (now foreign portfolio) investors and domestic institutional investors in Indian shares. Exchanges release provisional cash-market figures shortly after the close, showing each group's gross purchases, gross sales and net figure; NSDL separately publishes FPI flows across equity, debt and other instruments, based on custodian reports. Market reports read them as a sentiment gauge: sustained FII selling often coincides with a weaker rupee and falling large caps, while strong DII buying can absorb it. Traders also track FII positions in index futures and options, which are reported separately. Common confusion: net selling does not mean money left 'the market' as a whole, because every share sold has a buyer; it shows which group was on which side. Exchange and NSDL numbers also differ because they use different dates and coverage, such as primary-market purchases.
example: Say exchange data show FIIs bought ₹8,200 crore and sold ₹9,700 crore of shares, while DIIs bought ₹7,900 crore and sold ₹6,100 crore. FII net = ₹8,200 crore - ₹9,700 crore = -₹1,500 crore (net sellers); DII net = ₹7,900 crore - ₹6,100 crore = +₹1,800 crore (net buyers).
formula: Net flow = Gross purchases - Gross sales

short: Offshore instruments issued by registered foreign investors that let overseas investors share in the gains and losses of Indian shares without registering in India themselves.
kid: A friend who is allowed into the toy shop buys a toy and gives you a ticket saying you win too if the toy gets more popular. You never go into the shop yourself.
detail: Participatory notes (P-notes), a type of offshore derivative instrument (ODI), are issued outside India by SEBI-registered foreign portfolio investors, mostly global banks' brokerage arms, to overseas clients. The issuer holds the underlying Indian shares and passes their gains and losses on to the note holder, who never appears on the company's register. Popular in the 2000s, they once made up a large share of foreign holdings but raised concerns about anonymity and the round-tripping of Indian money through tax havens. SEBI has since tightened the rules: issuers must collect and report KYC details on note holders, and under the rules as of 2025 ODIs can no longer use derivatives as the underlying. P-notes now make up a small fraction of foreign investment. Common confusion: P-note holders are not shareholders of the company; they have no voting rights and do not appear in its shareholding pattern.
example: Say a fund abroad, not registered in India, wants $10 million of exposure to ABC Ltd. A registered FPI buys the shares and issues it a P-note; if ABC's shares rise 8%, the note is worth about $10 million x 1.08 = $10.8 million, ignoring currency moves and the issuer's fees, while ABC's register shows only the FPI.

short: In India, the founder, family or parent company that controls a company and is formally identified as its controlling group in filings.
kid: The girl who started the lemonade stand and still decides the recipe is its boss. Even when friends chip in, she keeps the biggest part and makes the big choices.
detail: In Indian company law and SEBI rules, a promoter is a person or entity that controls a company, directly or indirectly, or is named as a promoter in its offer document or annual return. Promoters are usually founders, their families or a parent company; the promoter group adds relatives and entities they control. Promoters carry extra responsibilities: in an IPO, part of their stake is locked in for a set period, they must disclose dealings and pledges, and their related-party transactions face extra scrutiny. Investors watch promoters closely because their integrity, holdings and actions often decide what minority shareholders get. Common confusion: a large shareholder is not automatically a promoter; an insurer owning 12% is still a public shareholder. Some well-known Indian companies are professionally managed and have no identified promoter at all. Outside India, the closer terms are controlling shareholder or founder.
example: Say the founding family of ABC Ltd and its holding company together own 54% of the shares, so they form the promoter group and the other 46% is public shareholding. If the family sells 6% to institutions, promoter holding falls to 54% - 6% = 48% and the public share rises to 52%.

short: The percentage of a company's shares owned by its promoter and promoter group, disclosed every quarter by Indian listed companies.
kid: If the girl who started the lemonade stand owns 6 of its 10 cups, she owns most of it. People watch whether she keeps her cups or gives them away.
detail: Promoter holding is the stake that the promoter and promoter group hold in a listed company, reported each quarter in the shareholding pattern filed with the stock exchanges. A high, stable holding is read as skin in the game: the people in control gain or lose alongside other shareholders. Rising holding, through open-market buying, a preferential allotment or a buyback, is often taken as a confidence signal; falling holding draws questions. Under SEBI's takeover rules as of 2025, a promoter group already owning at least 25% can buy up to 5% more each financial year without making an open offer, within the 75% ceiling implied by minimum public shareholding. Common confusion: a falling stake is not always bad news, since promoters may sell to meet public-shareholding rules, fund other ventures or settle estates; and a high stake means less if much of it is pledged.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 crore shares and the promoter group owns 6.2 crore of them, so promoter holding is 6.2 / 10 = 62%. If the company issues 0.5 crore new shares to outside investors, the holding falls to 6.2 / 10.5 = about 59.0%, even though the promoters sold nothing.
formula: Promoter holding (%) = Shares held by promoter and promoter group / Total shares outstanding x 100

short: Shares a promoter gives a lender as loan security; the lender may sell them if the loan goes unpaid or their value falls too far.
kid: You borrow your friend's bike and give her your favourite toy to hold until you bring the bike back. If you don't, she gets to keep the toy.
detail: Pledged shares are shares placed as collateral with a bank, NBFC or other lender, most often by promoters raising money for themselves or group companies. The shares stay in the promoter's name, but the lender has a claim on them. Loans are made against a cover ratio: if the share price falls, the lender asks for more shares or cash (a top-up); if that does not come, it can invoke the pledge and sell the shares in the market. Such forced selling can push the price lower, trigger further invocations and even shift control of the company. Indian listed companies disclose pledged promoter shares each quarter, and promoters must report new pledges promptly. A high pledge level, especially while shares are falling, is a widely used red flag. Common confusion: since 2020 investors also pledge shares to their broker for trading margin, which is a different, routine use.
example: Say a promoter pledges 1 crore shares worth ₹200 each (₹200 crore) for a ₹100 crore loan, so cover is ₹200 crore / ₹100 crore = 2 times. If the price falls to ₹120, the shares are worth ₹120 crore and cover drops to 1.2 times; if the lender requires, say, 1.5 times, it can demand more shares or invoke the pledge and sell.
formula: Pledged share % = Promoter shares pledged / Total promoter shares x 100 (also reported as a % of total shares)

short: Any pledge, lien, non-disposal promise or similar arrangement that restricts an owner's freedom to sell shares; wider than a simple pledge.
kid: Sometimes you promise a friend, 'I won't give my toy car to anyone else until I pay you back.' The car is still yours, but you are not free to give it away.
detail: In Indian securities rules, an encumbrance on shares is any arrangement that restricts the holder's right to sell or transfer them. It includes formal pledges and liens, and also non-disposal undertakings (NDUs), in which a promoter promises a lender not to sell or transfer shares without permission, with no pledge recorded in the depository. Because NDUs and other side arrangements could hide how much of a promoter's stake was tied to borrowing, SEBI widened disclosure rules in 2019: promoters must disclose all encumbrances and give reasons once encumbrance crosses set thresholds. Investors therefore look at total encumbered shares, not just pledged shares, to judge the risk that lenders could force a sale or a change of control. Common confusion: in property law, an encumbrance is a claim on land or a building, such as a mortgage, shown in an encumbrance certificate; the idea is similar but the context differs.
example: Say a promoter owns 4 crore shares of ABC Ltd: 1 crore are pledged to a bank and another 1.5 crore are under a non-disposal undertaking with a lender. Total encumbrance is 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 crore shares, or 2.5 / 4 = 62.5% of the promoter's holding, even though only 1 / 4 = 25% is formally pledged.
formula: Encumbrance % = Promoter shares pledged, under NDU or otherwise encumbered / Total promoter shares x 100

short: A quarterly table every Indian listed company files showing who owns its shares: promoters, mutual funds, foreign investors, other institutions and the public.
kid: Imagine a pie shared at a party, and a chart that shows how big a slice each person got. This chart does the same for the owners of a big shop.
detail: The shareholding pattern is a standard disclosure that listed companies in India file with the stock exchanges every quarter, under SEBI's listing rules as of 2025 generally within 21 days of the quarter's end. It splits ownership into the promoter and promoter group; public shareholders, divided into institutions (mutual funds, insurers, banks, foreign portfolio investors) and non-institutions (individuals, companies, NRIs and others); and non-promoter non-public holders such as employee benefit trusts. It also shows promoter shares that are pledged or encumbered and shares under lock-in. Analysts compare patterns quarter to quarter to see whether mutual funds or FPIs are buying, whether promoters are selling and how widely held a stock is. Common confusion: it is a snapshot as of the last day of the quarter, not a live record, so it can be about three weeks old when published and months old before the next one.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 20 crore shares. Its shareholding pattern shows promoters with 11 crore (11 / 20 = 55%), FPIs 3 crore (15%), mutual funds and other DIIs 4 crore (20%) and individuals and others 2 crore (10%), which adds up to 55 + 15 + 20 + 10 = 100%.

short: An Indian rule, as of 2025, that at least 25% of a listed company's shares be held by the public, capping promoters at 75%.
kid: If one child owns almost all the marbles, nobody else can really play. This rule says at least one in every four marbles must belong to other children, so the game stays fair.
detail: Minimum public shareholding (MPS) comes from the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, and is enforced by SEBI. Since 2010, listed companies have had to keep at least 25% of their shares with public shareholders, meaning anyone outside the promoter group, including individuals, mutual funds and FPIs. Very large companies listing for the first time may start with a smaller public float and get several years to reach 25%, and some government-owned companies have received extended deadlines. Companies that fall short can comply through an offer for sale by promoters, a qualified institutional placement, a rights or bonus issue in which promoters give up their entitlement, or similar routes; persistent non-compliance can bring fines, freezing of promoter shares and other action. The aim is enough free float for fair price discovery and less room for manipulation. Common confusion: public does not mean retail; institutional investors count as public too.
example: Say promoters own 82% of ABC Ltd, which has 10 crore shares, so public holding is 18%. To reach 25% public, the promoters must cut their stake to 75%, selling 7% of 10 crore = 70 lakh shares, for example through an offer for sale.
formula: Public shareholding (%) = Shares held by public shareholders / Total shares x 100; minimum required: 25% (rules as of 2025)

short: A first share sale by a small or mid-sized company on NSE Emerge or BSE SME, platforms with lighter rules than the main market.
kid: A tiny new lemonade stand asks neighbours to buy a part of it, at a special corner of the fair for small stands. It can grow fast, but it can also fold up quickly.
detail: An SME IPO is an initial public offering by a small or medium enterprise on a dedicated exchange segment: NSE Emerge or BSE SME, both launched in 2012. Eligibility and disclosure rules are lighter than for the main board: the offer document is vetted by the exchange rather than SEBI, issue sizes are small, and a market maker must provide buy and sell quotes after listing. Shares trade only in large lots. After frenzied, hugely oversubscribed issues in 2023-24 and cases of inflated financials and price manipulation, SEBI tightened the framework in 2025, adding requirements such as a profitability track record and larger minimum applications. Companies that grow can later migrate to the main board. Common confusion: being listed on an exchange does not make an SME stock as liquid or as closely scrutinised as a mainboard stock; trading can be thin and prices volatile.
example: Say XYZ Ltd lists on an SME platform at ₹100 a share with a lot of 1,200 shares, so one lot costs 1,200 x ₹100 = ₹1,20,000; under the rules as of 2025 an individual must apply for at least 2 lots, or ₹2,40,000. If the price falls 20% after listing, each lot is worth ₹96,000, and because trades happen only in whole lots of a thinly traded stock, it may be hard to sell quickly.

short: An initial public offering on the main segment of NSE and BSE, with SEBI-reviewed documents and stricter eligibility than the SME platforms.
kid: Big lemonade stands that the fair's rule-keeper has checked carefully get to sell parts of themselves in the main hall. Smaller stands use a side room.
detail: A mainboard IPO is a public offer of shares that lists on the main (non-SME) segment of NSE and BSE. The company files a draft red herring prospectus with SEBI, which must issue observations before the issue can open. Eligibility under SEBI's ICDR Regulations rests on a track record of net tangible assets, operating profit and net worth; companies that do not meet it can still list if at least 75% of the issue goes to qualified institutional buyers. Most mainboard IPOs are book-built within a price band, with set portions for retail individuals (bids up to ₹2 lakh under the rules as of 2025), non-institutional investors and QIBs, plus anchor investors who commit a day early. Under the T+3 timeline, also as of 2025, shares list three working days after the issue closes. Common confusion: SEBI's review checks disclosure, not price or quality; mainboard status guarantees nothing about returns.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a profitable company, raises ₹1,000 crore in a book-built mainboard IPO. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, at least 35% (₹350 crore) is set aside for retail investors, at least 15% (₹150 crore) for non-institutional investors and up to 50% (₹500 crore) for QIBs: ₹350 crore + ₹150 crore + ₹500 crore = ₹1,000 crore.

short: The unofficial premium over the issue price at which an IPO's shares are informally traded before they list, used as a rough gauge of demand.
kid: Before a new toy reaches the shops, some kids whisper, 'I would swap two sweets for it!' That whisper is a guess about how much the toy will be wanted, not a promise.
detail: The grey market premium (GMP) is the amount above the IPO issue price at which dealers in an unofficial, unregulated market offer to buy or sell an IPO's shares before listing. Deals are settled privately in cash once allotment and listing are known, outside any exchange. Two related quotes exist: kostak is a fixed sum paid for an application whether or not it gets an allotment, and subject to sauda is a price paid only if the application is allotted shares. Financial media widely report GMP as a hint of listing-day demand. Common confusion: GMP is not an official or reliable forecast. It comes from a thin, opaque network that can be manipulated to build hype, it can swing sharply within days, it often misses the actual listing price, and anyone dealing in it has no investor protection. SEBI has cautioned investors against relying on such unofficial dealings.
example: Say ABC Ltd's IPO is priced at ₹200 and the GMP is quoted at ₹50. That implies an expected listing price of ₹200 + ₹50 = ₹250, a 50 / 200 = 25% premium; but if sentiment sours before listing day, the shares may open at, say, ₹190, below the issue price.
formula: Implied listing price = Issue price + GMP; GMP % = GMP / Issue price x 100

short: The mandatory IPO payment method in India: your bid money stays in your bank account, blocked, and is debited only for shares you receive.
kid: You save sweets in a jar for a special treat, and Mum puts a lid on it so you can't eat them yet. If you don't get the treat, the lid comes off and the sweets are still all yours.
detail: ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount) is the system SEBI introduced in 2008 and made compulsory for all public issues from 2016. When you apply for an IPO, rights issue or similar offer, your bank blocks the application amount instead of sending it to the company. The money keeps earning savings interest but cannot be spent until allotment is decided; then only the amount for shares actually allotted is debited and the rest is released. Individual investors usually apply through their broker's app with a UPI mandate, which they must approve in their UPI app before bidding closes or the bid is invalid; SEBI sets an upper limit for UPI-based bids. Under the T+3 listing timeline as of 2025, unused funds are released within days. Common confusion: a block is not a debit, but it does tie up the money, so the same funds cannot back two applications.
example: Say you apply for 2 lots of an IPO at ₹15,000 per lot. ASBA blocks 2 x ₹15,000 = ₹30,000 in your bank account; if you are allotted 1 lot, ₹15,000 is debited and the other ₹15,000 is unblocked, and if you get nothing, the full ₹30,000 is released.

short: How many times investors' bids exceed the shares on offer in an IPO, reported overall and separately for each investor category.
kid: If a baker makes 10 cupcakes and 50 children ask for them, there are 5 children for every cupcake. That shows the cupcakes are very wanted, and most children won't get one.
detail: IPO subscription measures demand for a public issue: the number of shares bid for divided by the number offered, tracked live on exchange websites during the bidding period. It is shown separately for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), non-institutional investors (split into bids of ₹2-10 lakh and above ₹10 lakh under the rules as of 2025) and retail individual investors, with the anchor portion excluded. An issue 'subscribed 40 times' received bids for 40 times the shares available; below 1 time it is undersubscribed, and an issue that fails to reach the minimum subscription, usually 90% of the fresh issue, must refund the money. Heavy QIB demand is often read as a vote of confidence from professional investors. Common confusion: high subscription does not guarantee listing gains, and it is measured in shares bid, not number of applications; in a heavily subscribed retail book, your chance of allotment falls sharply.
example: Say ABC Ltd offers 1 crore shares to retail investors and receives retail bids for 25 crore shares. The retail portion is subscribed 25 / 1 = 25 times, so many applicants will get nothing, because each successful retail applicant usually receives just one lot.
formula: Subscription (times) = Shares bid for / Shares offered (overall or in each category)

short: The process of deciding which IPO applicants receive shares and how many, finalised by the registrar with the stock exchange after bidding closes.
kid: When more children want cupcakes than there are cupcakes, names go into a hat. Each name pulled out gets one cupcake, and everyone else gets their pocket money back.
detail: IPO allotment is the step after an issue closes in which the registrar (RTA), with the designated stock exchange, finalises the basis of allotment: who gets shares, and how many. QIB bids are allotted proportionately. For retail individual investors, SEBI rules aim to give as many applicants as possible the minimum bid lot: if valid applications exceed the lots available, lots are allotted by computerised lottery, one per winning applicant, and shares left over after that are allotted proportionately. Small non-institutional bids follow a similar minimum-application principle. Under the T+3 timeline as of 2025, allotment is usually finalised the day after the issue closes, shares are credited and money unblocked the next day, and listing follows on the third working day. Investors check allotment status on the registrar's or exchange's website. Common confusion: in an oversubscribed retail book, applying for more lots does not raise your chance of getting one.
example: Say an IPO's retail portion has 50,000 lots and receives 10 lakh valid retail applications. Since each lucky applicant gets one lot, the chance of allotment is 50,000 / 10,00,000 = 5%, or 1 in 20, whether you applied for 1 lot or the maximum.

short: The final IPO price set within the price band after bids are collected; retail investors can bid 'at cut-off' to accept whatever that price is.
kid: Kids say how many sweets they would give for a new toy, and the shop picks one fair number for everyone. Saying 'cut-off' means 'I'll give whatever number you pick'.
detail: In a book-built issue, investors bid within a price band, and after bidding closes the company and its bankers fix a single issue price, the cut-off price, at which shares are allotted, usually at or near the top of the band. Retail individual investors, and employees or shareholders bidding in reserved portions, may tick cut-off instead of naming a price, which means they agree to pay the final price, whatever it is. Their application amount is blocked at the upper end of the band, and any excess is released once the price is fixed. Institutional and other non-retail investors cannot bid at cut-off; they must quote a price, and a bid below the final price is rejected. Ticking cut-off is the simplest way to avoid a rejected bid. Common confusion: the cut-off price is not the lowest acceptable price but the final price every successful bidder pays.
example: Say an IPO has a price band of ₹270-₹285 and a lot of 52 shares. A retail investor who ticks cut-off has 52 x ₹285 = ₹14,820 blocked; if the final price is fixed at ₹280, they pay 52 x ₹280 = ₹14,560 and ₹14,820 - ₹14,560 = ₹260 is unblocked.
